level.name: Intermediate
level.description: Develop independent communication for travel, work, study, experiences, opinions, narratives, and common real-life situations.

topics.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
topics.objective: Choose between the present perfect and past simple when talking about experiences and finished past events.
topics.theory: Use the present perfect when the exact past time is not important or when the action connects to the present. Use the past simple when the time is finished or explicitly stated. Compare 'I have visited Rome' with 'I visited Rome in 2024'.
examples: I've seen that film twice.
I saw it last Friday.
She has worked here for three years.
She started here in 2023.

common_mistakes.wrong: I've visited Paris last year.
common_mistakes.correct: I visited Paris last year.

common_mistakes.wrong: Did you ever try sushi?
common_mistakes.correct: Have you ever tried sushi?

questions.prompt: Choose the best sentence.
questions.option_a: I've been to London last year.
questions.option_b: I went to London last year.
questions.option_c: I have gone to London last year.
questions.option_d: I did been to London last year.
questions.explanation: Use the past simple with a finished time such as 'last year'.

questions.prompt: Complete: ___ you ever ___ a marathon?
questions.explanation: Use present perfect for life experience without a finished time.

questions.prompt: Complete: She ___ that book three times.
questions.explanation: No finished time is stated; the experience matters.

questions.prompt: Complete: We ___ the project on Monday.
questions.explanation: Monday is a finished past time.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct pair.
questions.option_a: I've met him in 2022. / We have talked yesterday.
questions.option_b: I met him in 2022. / We talked yesterday.
questions.option_c: I have met him in 2022. / We talked yesterday.
questions.option_d: I met him in 2022. / We have talked yesterday.
questions.explanation: Both sentences use explicit finished times.

questions.prompt: Read: 'I've worked with Ana for two years. We met at a conference in Madrid.' Which event has a specific finished past time?
questions.explanation: The meeting is linked to a specific past event.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_b: She finished the course last month.
questions.explanation: Use 'We moved here in 2021.'

questions.prompt: Complete: I ___ my keys, so I can't open the door.
questions.explanation: The present result is important: the keys are still missing.

questions.prompt: Why can't the speaker enter the apartment?
questions.option_d: They are waiting for a friend
questions.explanation: The speaker says the keys are missing now.
questions.audio_text: I've lost my apartment keys, and I can't get inside. I think I left them at the café.

questions.prompt: When did the speaker visit Prague?
questions.explanation: The speaker gives a finished time.
questions.audio_text: I've been to Prague twice. The last time I went was last summer.

passages.title: Two Different Trips
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Which trip happened in a clearly finished past period?
questions.explanation: The Iceland trip is dated 2023 and described as completed.

questions.prompt: Why hasn't Daniel had much free time in Japan?
questions.explanation: He has attended meetings almost every day.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would be incorrect about the text?
questions.option_c: He hasn't had much free time.
questions.explanation: A finished time requires the past simple.

passages.content_text: Daniel has traveled abroad several times, but two trips stand out for different reasons. He went to Iceland in 2023 with three friends. They rented a car, drove around the south coast, and visited several waterfalls. The weather changed constantly, but Daniel says the trip was unforgettable. More recently, he has traveled to Japan for work. He has been there for ten days and has already visited Tokyo and Osaka. He hasn't had much free time because he has attended meetings almost every day. However, he has tried several local dishes and has learned a few useful expressions in Japanese. Daniel says Iceland felt like an adventure, while Japan has been a completely different experience because he is combining work and travel.

passages.title: A Career Update
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: When did the speaker change companies?
questions.explanation: The company change happened last September.

questions.prompt: What has the speaker already done with the new skills?
questions.explanation: The speaker has used the skills in two projects.

passages.audio_text: I've worked in marketing for five years, but I changed companies last September. Since then, I've learned a lot about digital advertising. I completed a short analytics course in January, and I've already used some of those skills in two projects. I haven't decided what course to take next.

topics.title: Present Perfect with For and Since
topics.objective: Use for and since to describe situations that started in the past and continue to the present.
topics.theory: Use 'for' with a period of time and 'since' with a starting point. Present perfect often appears with both: 'I've lived here for six years' and 'I've lived here since 2020'.
examples: We've known each other for a decade.
She's worked here since May.
I haven't seen him for two weeks.
How long have you lived here?

common_mistakes.wrong: I've lived here since five years.
common_mistakes.correct: I've lived here for five years.

common_mistakes.wrong: She's worked here for 2022.
common_mistakes.correct: She's worked here since 2022.

questions.prompt: Complete: I've lived here ___ 2019.
questions.explanation: 2019 is a starting point.

questions.prompt: Complete: She's studied English ___ three years.
questions.explanation: Three years is a period.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: We've known them since a long time.
questions.option_b: We've known them for a long time.
questions.option_c: We know them for a long time ago.
questions.option_d: We've knew them for a long time.
questions.explanation: Use for with a period of time.

questions.prompt: Complete: How long ___ you ___ here?
questions.explanation: Use present perfect to ask about duration continuing now.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option: 'He has worked remotely ___ March.'
questions.explanation: March is a starting point.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Nina started university in 2024 and she is still there.' Which sentence matches?
questions.explanation: Use since with the starting year.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.explanation: Use 'since 2020'.

questions.prompt: Complete: I haven't eaten anything ___ this morning.
questions.explanation: This morning is a starting point.

questions.prompt: How long has the speaker worked at the company?
questions.explanation: The speaker says three years.
questions.audio_text: I've worked at this company for three years, and I've been in my current team since January.

questions.prompt: Since when has the café been open?
questions.explanation: The speaker gives 2010 as the starting point.
questions.audio_text: This café has been open since 2010, and my family has managed it for more than a decade.

passages.title: A Long Friendship
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How long have they lived in different cities?
questions.explanation: The text says for the last six years.

questions.prompt: Since when has Hannah worked in Manchester?
questions.explanation: The text states since 2021.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_b: They haven't met for eight months.
questions.option_c: Lucy has lived in Bristol for four years.
questions.explanation: Use 'since 2021'.

passages.content_text: Lucy and Hannah have been close friends since secondary school. They first met when they were thirteen, and they have stayed in touch ever since. For the last six years, they have lived in different cities, but they still speak every week. Hannah has worked as a nurse in Manchester since 2021, while Lucy has lived in Bristol for four years. They haven't seen each other in person for eight months because their schedules have been busy. Next month, however, they are planning a weekend together. Lucy says their friendship has changed over time, but it has remained important to both of them.

passages.title: Learning a Skill
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: How long has the speaker owned the current camera?
questions.explanation: The speaker says for two years.

questions.prompt: Since when has the speaker taken the online course?
questions.explanation: The course has continued since February.

passages.audio_text: I've been interested in photography since I was a teenager. I've owned my current camera for two years, and I've taken an online course since February. I haven't finished it yet, but I've practiced regularly for several months.

topics.title: Past Continuous
topics.objective: Describe actions that were in progress at a particular moment in the past.
topics.theory: Form the past continuous with was/were + verb-ing. It is often used for background actions, actions in progress at a specific past time, and situations interrupted by another event.
examples: I was driving at eight.
They were studying when I called.
She wasn't sleeping.
Were you waiting for me?

common_mistakes.wrong: I was drive.
common_mistakes.correct: I was driving.

common_mistakes.wrong: They was working.
common_mistakes.correct: They were working.

questions.prompt: Complete: At 9 p.m., I ___ a report.
questions.explanation: The action was in progress at a specific past time.

questions.prompt: Complete: They ___ dinner when I arrived.
questions.explanation: Use were + verb-ing with they.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct negative.
questions.explanation: Use wasn't + verb-ing.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct question.
questions.explanation: Use Were + subject + verb-ing.

questions.prompt: Complete: While I was cooking, my brother ___ TV.
questions.explanation: Two actions were in progress simultaneously.

questions.prompt: Read: 'At midnight, people were still dancing.' What does this emphasize?
questions.explanation: Past continuous shows an action in progress.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.explanation: Use 'They were driving'.

questions.prompt: Complete: What ___ you ___ when the lights went out?
questions.explanation: Use past continuous for the interrupted action.

questions.prompt: What was the speaker doing when the phone rang?
questions.explanation: The speaker was cooking.
questions.audio_text: I was cooking dinner when my phone rang, so I turned the stove down before I answered.

questions.prompt: What were the children doing at five?
questions.explanation: They were playing outside.
questions.audio_text: At five o'clock, the children were playing outside while their parents were preparing dinner.

passages.title: The Power Cut
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What was the writer doing when the power went off?
questions.explanation: The writer was working on a laptop.

questions.prompt: What were the upstairs neighbors doing?
questions.explanation: They were cooking dinner.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: People were talking in the hallway.
questions.option_d: The family was watch a film.
questions.explanation: Use 'was watching'.

passages.content_text: Last Friday evening, several people in our building were doing different things when the electricity suddenly went off. I was working on my laptop in the living room. My neighbors upstairs were cooking dinner, and the family across the hall was watching a film. For a few seconds, nobody knew what had happened. People opened their doors and started talking in the hallway. While we were waiting for the lights to return, someone used a phone flashlight to check the electrical panel. The power came back after about twenty minutes. Fortunately, nobody was hurt, but one neighbor had been baking a cake and was worried about the oven.

passages.title: An Interrupted Meeting
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What were they discussing?
questions.explanation: They were discussing the monthly budget.

questions.prompt: What did the manager explain?
questions.explanation: The manager said it was only a test.

passages.audio_text: We were discussing the monthly budget when the fire alarm started. Everyone stopped talking and left the meeting room. While we were walking downstairs, the building manager told us it was only a test.

topics.title: Past Simple vs Past Continuous
topics.objective: Combine past simple and past continuous to describe interrupted actions and background events.
topics.theory: Use the past continuous for an action already in progress and the past simple for the shorter event that interrupts or changes it. 'I was walking home when it started to rain.'
examples: She was driving when the car broke down.
While I was studying, my friend called.
They arrived while we were eating.
I dropped my phone while I was running.

common_mistakes.wrong: I was walked when it rained.
common_mistakes.correct: I was walking when it started to rain.

common_mistakes.wrong: While I cooked, the phone was ringing once.
common_mistakes.correct: While I was cooking, the phone rang.

questions.prompt: Complete: I ___ home when I ___ an accident.
questions.explanation: The driving was in progress; seeing the accident was the shorter event.

questions.prompt: Complete: While they ___, it ___ to snow.
questions.explanation: Use past continuous for background and past simple for the event.

questions.prompt: Choose the best sentence.
questions.option_a: I read when she was calling.
questions.option_b: I was reading when she called.
questions.option_c: I was read when she called.
questions.option_d: I read while she called for hours.
questions.explanation: The ongoing action is 'was reading'.

questions.prompt: Complete: The lights went out while we ___ dinner.
questions.explanation: The dinner was in progress.

questions.prompt: Which clause usually describes the interruption?
questions.explanation: The shorter interrupting event is commonly past simple.

questions.prompt: Read: 'While Marta was cycling, she heard a strange noise.' Which action was already in progress?
questions.option_c: Both began at exactly the same instant
questions.explanation: Cycling was the ongoing background action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_a: I was sleeping when you called.
questions.option_b: While we were eating, the doorbell rang.
questions.option_c: They were played football when it started raining.
questions.option_d: He fell while he was skiing.
questions.explanation: Use 'were playing'.

questions.prompt: Complete: She ___ her ankle while she ___.
questions.explanation: The injury is the shorter event; running was in progress.

questions.prompt: What happened while the speaker was walking?
questions.explanation: Rain started during the walk.
questions.audio_text: I was walking to the station when it suddenly started raining, so I ran into a shop.

questions.prompt: What interrupted the meeting?
questions.explanation: The fire alarm interrupted it.
questions.audio_text: We were having our weekly meeting when the fire alarm went off.

passages.title: A Bicycle Accident
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What caused Nina to lose her balance?
questions.explanation: A car door opened as she approached.

questions.prompt: Who came to help?
questions.explanation: A passerby came to help.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_d: She was fell from the bicycle.
questions.explanation: Use 'She fell' or 'She was falling', depending on meaning.

passages.content_text: On Tuesday morning, Nina was cycling to work along a quiet street. The sun was shining, and traffic was moving slowly. As she was approaching an intersection, a car suddenly opened its door. Nina tried to stop, but she lost her balance and fell. A passerby was walking nearby and immediately came to help. While Nina was checking her arm, the driver got out and apologized. Luckily, she wasn't seriously injured, but her bicycle wheel was damaged. She called her office while she was waiting for a taxi and explained what had happened.

passages.title: A Missed Stop
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Why did the speaker miss the stop?
questions.explanation: The speaker was reading and not paying attention.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker do next?
questions.explanation: The speaker got off at the next stop and walked back.

passages.audio_text: I was reading an article on the bus when I realized we had passed my stop. I wasn't paying attention to the route because the article was interesting. I got off at the next stop and walked back.

topics.title: First Conditional
topics.objective: Talk about realistic future possibilities and their likely results.
topics.theory: Form the first conditional with if + present simple, will + base verb. The clauses can change order. Other modals or imperatives may sometimes appear in the result clause.
examples: If it rains, we'll stay inside.
I'll call you if I arrive early.
If you study, you'll improve.
If you see Marta, tell her to call me.

common_mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we'll stay home.
common_mistakes.correct: If it rains, we'll stay home.

common_mistakes.wrong: If you study, you will improves.
common_mistakes.correct: If you study, you will improve.

questions.prompt: Complete: If it ___ tomorrow, we'll cancel the picnic.
questions.explanation: Use present simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: Complete: I'll call you if I ___ late.
questions.explanation: Use present simple after if.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: If she studies, she will pass.
questions.option_b: If she will study, she passes.
questions.option_c: If she studied, she will pass.
questions.option_d: If she studies, she will passes.
questions.explanation: This is the standard first conditional form.

questions.prompt: Complete: If we miss the bus, we ___ a taxi.
questions.explanation: Use will for the likely future result.

questions.prompt: Meaning of 'unless' in 'Unless you hurry, you'll miss the train.'
questions.explanation: Unless means 'if not'.

questions.prompt: Read: 'If the weather is good, we'll eat outside.' What must happen for them to eat outside?
questions.explanation: Good weather is the condition.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_b: We'll go if we finish early.
questions.option_c: If he will come, I'll tell you.
questions.explanation: Do not normally use will in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: Complete: If you don't save the file, you ___ your changes.
questions.explanation: The likely future result uses will.

questions.prompt: What will they do if the train is delayed?
questions.explanation: They will take a bus.
questions.audio_text: If the train is delayed by more than an hour, we'll take the bus instead.

questions.prompt: What will happen if the speaker finishes early?
questions.explanation: The speaker will call.
questions.audio_text: If I finish work early, I'll call you and we can have dinner together.

passages.title: A Weather-Dependent Event
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Where will the film be shown if the weather stays dry?
questions.explanation: The outdoor plan is the park.

questions.prompt: Why should visitors arrive early if the event moves indoors?
questions.explanation: Indoor seating is more limited.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: If it rains, they'll move inside.
questions.option_b: If it stays dry, the film will start at eight.
questions.option_c: If visitors arrive early, they may find seats.
questions.option_d: If it will rain, they will cancel the website.
questions.explanation: Use present simple in the if-clause.

passages.content_text: Our community is planning an outdoor film night on Saturday. If the weather stays dry, the film will start at eight in the park. People can bring blankets and snacks. If it rains, the organizers will move the event to the community hall. If that happens, there will be fewer seats, so visitors will need to arrive early. The organizers say they will post a final update online at four in the afternoon. If you don't check the website, you may not know where the event is taking place.

passages.title: Work Deadline
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: When will the client review the report if it is finished on time?
questions.explanation: The client will review it Friday.

questions.prompt: What will happen if the client requests changes?
questions.explanation: They will update it on Monday.

passages.audio_text: If we finish the report by Thursday, the client will review it on Friday. If they ask for changes, we'll update it on Monday. Unless there are major problems, we'll send the final version next week.

topics.title: Second Conditional
topics.objective: Discuss hypothetical, unlikely, or imaginary present and future situations.
topics.theory: Use if + past simple, would + base verb for hypothetical situations. 'If I had more time, I would travel more.' The form 'were' is common with all subjects in more formal English, especially 'If I were you'.
examples: If I had more money, I'd travel.
If she knew the answer, she'd tell us.
What would you do if you lost your phone?
If I were you, I'd wait.

common_mistakes.wrong: If I would have time, I'd help.
common_mistakes.correct: If I had time, I'd help.

common_mistakes.wrong: If he had a car, he will drive.
common_mistakes.correct: If he had a car, he would drive.

questions.prompt: Complete: If I ___ more free time, I'd learn Italian.
questions.explanation: Use past simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: Complete: She would travel more if she ___ more money.
questions.explanation: Use past simple after if.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: If I were you, I'd apologize.
questions.option_b: If I would be you, I apologize.
questions.option_c: If I am you, I'd apologized.
questions.option_d: If I was you, I will apologize always.
questions.explanation: 'If I were you' is the standard advice form.

questions.prompt: Complete: What ___ you do if you won a free trip?
questions.explanation: Use would in the result question.

questions.prompt: Which situation is most likely hypothetical?
questions.option_a: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay in.
questions.option_b: If I were a millionaire, I'd buy a house by the sea.
questions.option_c: If you heat ice, it melts.
questions.option_d: I went home because I was tired.
questions.explanation: This is imaginary or unlikely.

questions.prompt: Read: 'If Mark lived closer, he would visit more often.' What is implied?
questions.explanation: The conditional suggests he currently lives farther away.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_a: If I had a car, I'd drive.
questions.option_c: If he would study, he'd improve.
questions.option_d: What would you buy if you won?
questions.explanation: Use 'If he studied'.

questions.prompt: Complete: If we ___ near the beach, we'd swim every day.
questions.explanation: Use past simple in the if-clause.

questions.prompt: What would the speaker do with more free time?
questions.explanation: The speaker would learn to cook.
questions.audio_text: If I had more free time, I'd take a cooking course and learn to make better meals.

questions.prompt: What advice is given?
questions.explanation: The speaker says 'If I were you'.
questions.audio_text: If I were you, I'd talk to your manager before making any big decision.

passages.title: A Different Career
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What career would James probably choose?
questions.explanation: He says he would probably become a teacher.

questions.prompt: What is one concern about changing careers?
questions.option_b: It would require training and lower initial pay
questions.explanation: Training and salary are concerns.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: If he changed careers, he'd need training.
questions.option_b: If money were not a concern, he'd consider it.
questions.option_c: If he would choose again, he'd become a teacher.
questions.explanation: Use 'If he chose again'.

passages.content_text: James sometimes imagines having a completely different career. He works in finance, but if he could choose again, he would probably become a teacher. He enjoys explaining ideas and helping younger colleagues at work. If he became a teacher, he says he would teach economics or mathematics. However, he knows that changing careers would require more training and a lower salary at first. If money were not a concern, he would consider the change more seriously.

passages.title: Dream Home
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Where would the speaker like to live?
questions.explanation: The speaker mentions the mountains.

questions.prompt: What would the speaker probably get if there were a large garden?
questions.explanation: The speaker says probably a dog.

passages.audio_text: If I could choose any place to live, I'd move somewhere near the mountains. I'd work remotely, grow vegetables, and spend more time outdoors. If the house had a large garden, I'd probably get a dog too.

topics.title: Obligation, Necessity, and Prohibition
topics.objective: Use must, have to, don't have to, and mustn't to talk about rules and necessity.
topics.theory: Use must and have to for obligation, though context and tone differ. 'Don't have to' means there is no necessity. 'Mustn't' means something is prohibited.
examples: You must wear a seat belt.
I have to finish this today.
You don't have to come early.
You mustn't smoke here.

common_mistakes.wrong: You don't have to park here. = Parking is prohibited.
common_mistakes.correct: You mustn't park here. = Parking is prohibited.

common_mistakes.wrong: I must to leave.
common_mistakes.correct: I must leave.

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses prohibition?
questions.explanation: Mustn't means prohibited.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means something is optional?
questions.explanation: Don't have to means no necessity.

questions.prompt: Complete: Employees ___ wear identification badges.
questions.explanation: This expresses workplace necessity.

questions.prompt: Complete: Visitors ___ take photographs in this area. It's forbidden.
questions.explanation: Mustn't expresses prohibition.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form.
questions.explanation: Use base verb after must.

questions.prompt: Read: 'You don't have to book in advance, but it is recommended.' What does this mean?
questions.explanation: There is no obligation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_a: We have to leave by six.
questions.option_b: You mustn't use your phone here.
questions.option_c: She has to wear a uniform.
questions.explanation: Modal 'must' does not take -s.

questions.prompt: Complete: Because the office is closed Friday, we ___ come in.
questions.explanation: There is no need to come in.

questions.prompt: What must visitors do?
questions.explanation: Visitors must wear a badge.
questions.audio_text: All visitors must wear a badge while they are inside the building.

questions.prompt: What is prohibited?
questions.option_b: Parking in front of the gate
questions.explanation: The speaker says parking there is prohibited.
questions.audio_text: You mustn't park in front of the gate because emergency vehicles need access.

passages.title: Office Rules
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: When do employees have to be available?
questions.explanation: They must be available between ten and three.

questions.prompt: What mustn't employees share?
questions.explanation: They mustn't share passwords.

questions.prompt: Which statement is incorrect in form?
questions.option_b: Employees don't have to arrive at eight.
questions.option_d: Everyone must to wear a badge.
questions.explanation: Use 'must wear'.

passages.content_text: Employees at Northbridge Design have a flexible schedule, but there are several important rules. Staff have to be available between ten and three for meetings. They don't have to arrive at eight every morning, and they can sometimes work from home. However, everyone must protect confidential client information. Employees mustn't share passwords or leave sensitive documents on their desks overnight. Visitors have to sign in at reception and wear a temporary badge. They don't have to be accompanied in the café area, but they must stay with a staff member in the main offices.

passages.title: Gym Instructions
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What does the gym provide?
questions.explanation: The gym provides a towel.

questions.prompt: Where mustn't people leave bags?
questions.explanation: Bags must not be left near equipment.

passages.audio_text: You have to bring clean indoor shoes into the exercise area. You don't have to bring a towel because the gym provides one. You mustn't leave bags near the equipment, and you must return weights after using them.

topics.title: Gerunds and Infinitives
topics.objective: Use common verb patterns with gerunds and infinitives.
topics.theory: Some verbs are followed by -ing, such as enjoy, avoid, finish, and suggest. Others are followed by to + infinitive, such as want, decide, hope, plan, and need. Some verbs allow both with differences or little change in meaning.
examples: I enjoy reading.
She decided to leave.
We hope to travel.
He finished writing the report.

common_mistakes.wrong: I enjoy to swim.
common_mistakes.correct: I enjoy swimming.

common_mistakes.wrong: She decided going home.
common_mistakes.correct: She decided to go home.

questions.prompt: Complete: I enjoy ___ in the morning.
questions.explanation: Enjoy is followed by a gerund.

questions.prompt: Complete: She decided ___ the offer.
questions.explanation: Decide is followed by to + infinitive.

questions.prompt: Complete: We hope ___ you soon.
questions.explanation: Hope is followed by to + infinitive.

questions.prompt: Complete: He finished ___ the presentation.
questions.explanation: Finish is followed by -ing.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_b: They avoided to drive at night.
questions.explanation: Avoid is followed by a gerund.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Maya plans to study abroad but avoids flying when possible.' Which verb is followed by an infinitive?
questions.explanation: Plan is followed by to + infinitive.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.explanation: Use 'decided to leave'.

questions.prompt: Complete: They suggested ___ earlier.
questions.explanation: Suggest is followed by a gerund.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker enjoy doing?
questions.explanation: The speaker enjoys cooking.
questions.audio_text: I enjoy cooking for friends, but I hate washing all the dishes afterward.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker decide to do?
questions.explanation: The speaker decided to change jobs.
questions.audio_text: After several difficult months, I decided to look for a new job.

passages.title: Changing Habits
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did Priya decide to change?
questions.explanation: She decided to change her routine.

questions.prompt: What does she enjoy doing before sleep?
questions.explanation: She enjoys reading.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is incorrect?
questions.explanation: Use 'hopes to join'.

passages.content_text: After years of working late, Priya decided to change her routine. She started going to bed earlier and stopped checking work email after nine. She enjoys reading before sleep because it helps her relax. She also plans to exercise three times a week and hopes to join a weekend hiking group. At first, she found it difficult to avoid looking at her phone, but after a few weeks it became easier. Priya says she wants to continue improving her routine because she has more energy now.

topics.title: Defining Relative Clauses
topics.objective: Use who, which, and that to add essential information about people and things.
topics.theory: Use who for people, which for things, and that for people or things in many defining relative clauses. These clauses identify exactly which person or thing we mean.
examples: The woman who called is my manager.
The book that you lent me was excellent.
This is the café which opened last week.
People who work remotely need good internet.

common_mistakes.wrong: The woman which called me.
common_mistakes.correct: The woman who called me.

common_mistakes.wrong: The computer who broke.
common_mistakes.correct: The computer that broke.

questions.prompt: Choose: The man ___ lives next door is a doctor.
questions.explanation: Use who for people.

questions.prompt: Choose: The laptop ___ I bought is very light.
questions.explanation: Use which for a thing.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.option_a: The woman which called is here.
questions.option_b: The woman who called is here.
questions.option_c: The woman where called is here.
questions.option_d: The woman what called is here.
questions.explanation: Use who for a person.

questions.prompt: Complete: This is the film ___ everyone recommended.
questions.explanation: That can refer to things in defining clauses.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: People who work here get free lunch.
questions.option_b: People which work here get free lunch.
questions.option_c: People where work here get free lunch.
questions.option_d: People what work here get free lunch.
questions.explanation: Use who for people.

questions.prompt: Read: 'The app that I use for budgeting is free.' What does the relative clause identify?
questions.explanation: It tells us which app.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_a: The student who won is absent.
questions.option_b: The phone that I ordered arrived.
questions.option_c: The person which helped me was kind.
questions.option_d: The book which I borrowed is here.
questions.explanation: Use who/that for a person.

questions.prompt: Complete: The restaurant ___ serves vegan food is near here.
questions.explanation: That refers to the restaurant.

questions.prompt: Who is the speaker describing?
questions.option_a: A colleague who speaks three languages
questions.explanation: The description is of a multilingual colleague.
questions.audio_text: I work with a colleague who speaks Spanish, French, and English fluently.

questions.prompt: What is being described?
questions.explanation: The speaker describes a website.
questions.audio_text: I found a website that compares hotel prices from several travel companies.

questions.option_b: A friend who works in IT
questions.explanation: The writer's IT friend recommended it.

questions.prompt: What can urgent customers sometimes receive the same day?
questions.explanation: Urgent repairs may be completed the same day.

questions.prompt: Which clause is incorrect?
questions.option_a: the owner who has worked there
questions.option_d: a friend which works in IT

passages.content_text: There's a small repair shop near my office that has become very popular. The owner, who has worked with electronics for more than twenty years, repairs phones, laptops, and tablets. Customers who need urgent repairs can sometimes get their devices back on the same day. The shop also sells refurbished computers that are cheaper than new ones. A friend who works in IT recommended the place to me after my laptop screen broke. The technician who helped me explained the problem clearly and repaired it within two days.

topics.title: Passive Voice: Present and Past
topics.objective: Use the passive voice when the action or result is more important than the person who performs it.
topics.theory: Form the passive with be + past participle. Present simple passive: is/are + participle. Past simple passive: was/were + participle. Use by when the agent is important.
examples: The emails are sent every morning.
The bridge was built in 1998.
English is spoken here.
The report was prepared by Ana.

common_mistakes.wrong: The report was prepare.
common_mistakes.correct: The report was prepared.

common_mistakes.wrong: Cars are make here.
common_mistakes.correct: Cars are made here.

questions.prompt: Complete: Coffee ___ in many countries.
questions.explanation: Present passive: is + past participle.

questions.prompt: Complete: The building ___ in 2005.
questions.explanation: Past passive: was + participle.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: Plural present passive uses are + participle.

questions.prompt: Complete: The invitations ___ yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past plural passive uses were sent.

questions.prompt: Which sentence focuses on the result rather than the agent?
questions.option_b: The report was written by Ana.
questions.explanation: The passive puts the report first.

questions.prompt: Read: 'The museum was renovated in 2022.' What is emphasized?
questions.explanation: The museum and renovation are foregrounded.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_d: The product is make in Italy.
questions.explanation: Use 'is made'.

questions.prompt: Complete: These documents ___ by the manager every Friday.
questions.explanation: Use present passive for a regular process.

questions.prompt: When was the station renovated?
questions.explanation: The speaker says 2022.
questions.audio_text: The old station was renovated in 2022, and a new ticket hall was added.

questions.prompt: What is produced at the factory?
questions.explanation: The factory produces bicycles.
questions.audio_text: More than five hundred bicycles are produced at this factory every week.

passages.title: How Coffee Reaches the Cup
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What happens after the beans are picked?
questions.explanation: They are processed and dried.

questions.prompt: Where are the beans roasted?
questions.explanation: They are transported and then roasted.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_a: Coffee is grown in tropical regions.
questions.option_d: The beans are package and sent.
questions.explanation: Use 'are packaged'.

passages.content_text: Coffee is grown in many tropical regions around the world. After the beans are picked, they are processed and dried. They are then transported to other countries, where they are roasted. Different temperatures are used to create different flavors. After roasting, the beans are packaged and sent to shops, cafés, and restaurants. In many cafés, the beans are ground immediately before the coffee is prepared. Although machines are used for several stages, many important decisions are still made by people with specialist knowledge.

topics.title: Reported Speech: Statements
topics.objective: Report what someone said without repeating the exact words.
topics.theory: In reported speech, pronouns, time expressions, and verb forms may change depending on context. A common pattern is said (that) + clause. For example: 'I'm tired' → She said that she was tired.
examples: 'I'm busy.' → He said he was busy.
'We live here.' → They said they lived there.
'I can't come.' → She said she couldn't come.
He told me he was leaving.

common_mistakes.wrong: She said me she was tired.
common_mistakes.correct: She told me she was tired. / She said she was tired.

common_mistakes.wrong: He said that he is tired yesterday.
common_mistakes.correct: He said that he was tired.

questions.prompt: Report: 'I'm tired.'
questions.option_d: She told that she is tired.
questions.explanation: A common backshift is am → was.

questions.prompt: Report: 'We can't come.'
questions.explanation: Can commonly changes to could.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: He said me he was busy.
questions.option_b: He told me he was busy.
questions.option_c: He told that he was busy me.
questions.option_d: He said to me that busy.
questions.explanation: Tell usually takes an object: told me.

questions.prompt: Report: 'I will call you.'
questions.option_a: She said she would call me.
questions.option_b: She said she will called me.
questions.explanation: Will often changes to would.

questions.prompt: Which reporting verb normally requires an object?
questions.explanation: Tell is normally followed by a person.

questions.prompt: Read: Maya said, 'I don't know the answer.' Which report is correct?
questions.option_a: Maya said she didn't know the answer.
questions.explanation: This is the standard reported form.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_b: She told me she was busy.
questions.option_d: He said me he was tired.
questions.explanation: Use 'told me' or 'said he...'.

questions.prompt: Report: 'We are working from home.'
questions.option_a: They said they were working from home.
questions.option_b: They said they work from home yesterday.
questions.explanation: Are working commonly backshifts to were working.

questions.prompt: What did Clara say?
questions.explanation: The speaker reports Clara's message.
questions.audio_text: Clara called and said she was running about fifteen minutes late.

questions.prompt: What did the manager tell the team?
questions.explanation: The deadline moved.
questions.audio_text: The manager told us that the deadline had moved from Thursday to Friday.

questions.option_d: Emma said Ryan that the client was happy.

passages.content_text: Ryan couldn't attend the morning meeting, so his colleague Emma called him afterward. She said the client was happy with the first design but wanted a few changes. She told Ryan that the colors needed to be simpler and that the home page should include less text. Emma also said the client would send new photographs later that afternoon. Ryan thanked her and said he would update the design before the next meeting.

topics.title: Future Forms: Will, Going To, and Present Continuous
topics.objective: Choose among common future forms for predictions, intentions, spontaneous decisions, and arrangements.
topics.theory: Use going to for prior intentions and evidence-based predictions, present continuous for fixed arrangements, and will for spontaneous decisions, promises, offers, and some predictions.
examples: I'm meeting Sara at six.
We're going to repaint the kitchen.
I'll answer the phone.
I think prices will rise.

common_mistakes.wrong: I'm going to meeting them at six.
common_mistakes.correct: I'm meeting them at six. / I'm going to meet them at six.

common_mistakes.wrong: I will going to call him.
common_mistakes.correct: I'll call him. / I'm going to call him.

questions.prompt: You arranged dinner yesterday. Choose the best sentence.
questions.option_a: I'm meeting Ana for dinner tonight.
questions.option_b: I'll meet Ana perhaps now decision.
questions.explanation: Present continuous is common for fixed arrangements.

questions.prompt: You decide now to answer the phone.
questions.option_a: I'm going to answer it next year.
questions.explanation: Will is common for spontaneous decisions.

questions.prompt: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
questions.explanation: Present evidence supports a going-to prediction.

questions.prompt: Complete: We ___ the dentist at 3 p.m. tomorrow; the appointment is booked.
questions.explanation: Present continuous expresses a fixed arrangement.

questions.prompt: Choose the best sentence for an intention already decided.
questions.option_a: I'm going to start a course next month.
questions.option_b: I'll start a course, decision made months ago is impossible.
questions.explanation: Going to fits a prior intention.

questions.prompt: Read: 'I forgot my wallet.' 'Don't worry, I'll pay.' Why is will used?
questions.explanation: The decision is made at the moment.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_c: We're going to move next year.
questions.option_d: I'm going to meeting my manager.
questions.explanation: Use 'going to meet'.

questions.prompt: Complete: They ___ us at the station at 8. Everything is arranged.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker decide at the moment?
questions.option_c: To book a flight next year
questions.explanation: The decision is spontaneous.
questions.audio_text: You look tired. I'll make some coffee for both of us.

He hasn't booked anything for Wednesday, but he thinks he'll probably work late because a project deadline is close. On Thursday, he's having dinner with his sister. When she called yesterday, she mentioned she was moving apartment, so Martin said, 'I'll help you this weekend.'

topics.title: Common Phrasal Verbs
topics.objective: Understand and use common phrasal verbs in everyday contexts.
topics.theory: Phrasal verbs combine a verb with a particle. Their meaning may be literal or idiomatic. Common B1 examples include find out, look after, give up, turn on, turn off, pick up, run out of, and look for.
examples: I found out the truth.
Can you look after my dog?
We ran out of milk.
I'll pick you up at six.

common_mistakes.wrong: We ran milk out of.
common_mistakes.correct: We ran out of milk.

common_mistakes.wrong: I look my keys for.
common_mistakes.correct: I'm looking for my keys.

questions.prompt: What does 'look after' mean?
questions.explanation: Look after means take care of.

questions.prompt: What does 'run out of' mean?
questions.explanation: It means there is no more of something.

questions.prompt: Complete: I'll ___ you ___ at the station.
questions.explanation: Pick someone up means collect them.

questions.prompt: What does 'find out' mean?
questions.explanation: Find out means discover.

questions.prompt: If you 'give up' a difficult task, you...
questions.explanation: Give up means stop trying.

questions.prompt: Read: 'We ran out of printer paper, so I went to buy more.' What happened?

questions.prompt: Complete: Can you ___ the lights before you leave?

passages.title: A Day of Small Problems
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What did the writer run out of?

questions.prompt: What did the manager ask the writer to find out?
questions.option_b: Why a client hadn't received an email
questions.explanation: The manager wanted the email problem investigated.

questions.prompt: Which meaning is incorrect in context?
questions.option_a: run out of = have none left
questions.explanation: Pick up does not mean stop trying.

passages.content_text: Yesterday seemed to be full of small problems. First, I ran out of coffee before breakfast, so I had to stop at a café on the way to work. At the office, I couldn't find my access card and spent ten minutes looking for it. Then my manager asked me to find out why a client hadn't received an email. During lunch, my sister called and asked if I could look after her dog this weekend. By the afternoon, I felt like giving up, but things improved. I found my access card inside my notebook, solved the email problem, and remembered to pick up coffee on the way home.

topics.title: Expressing Opinions and Linking Ideas
topics.objective: Organize spoken and written ideas using common linking words and opinion expressions.
topics.theory: Use expressions such as in my opinion, I think, I agree, I disagree, because, although, however, so, therefore, and for example to organize ideas and show relationships.
examples: In my opinion, public transport should be cheaper.
I agree because it would reduce traffic.
Although the job is demanding, I enjoy it.
The bus was late, so I took a taxi.

common_mistakes.wrong: Although it was raining, but we went out.
common_mistakes.correct: Although it was raining, we went out.

common_mistakes.wrong: I was tired however I finished.
common_mistakes.correct: I was tired; however, I finished.

questions.prompt: Which phrase introduces a personal view?
questions.explanation: In my opinion introduces a viewpoint.

questions.prompt: Complete: I stayed home ___ I was feeling sick.
questions.explanation: Because gives the reason.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.option_a: Although it was expensive, I bought it.
questions.option_b: Although it was expensive, but I bought it.
questions.option_c: Although because it was expensive, I bought it.
questions.explanation: Do not normally combine although and but in the same structure.

questions.prompt: Which linker shows contrast?
questions.explanation: However signals contrast.

questions.prompt: Complete: The train was canceled, ___ we took a bus.
questions.explanation: So expresses a result.

questions.prompt: Read: 'I enjoy remote work. However, I sometimes miss seeing colleagues.' What relationship does 'however' show?
questions.explanation: The second idea contrasts with the first.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains an error?
questions.option_a: I agree because the plan is practical.
questions.option_b: Although it was late, we continued.
questions.option_c: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
questions.option_d: Although I was tired, but I finished.
questions.explanation: Do not use both although and but in this pattern.

questions.prompt: Which phrase introduces an example?
questions.explanation: For example introduces an illustration.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's opinion?
questions.explanation: The speaker states this opinion.
questions.audio_text: In my opinion, public transport should be cheaper because it would encourage more people to leave their cars at home.

questions.prompt: Why does the second speaker disagree?
questions.explanation: Cost is the reason.
questions.audio_text: I understand the idea; however, I disagree because the proposal would be too expensive for the city.

passages.title: Should Offices Be Fully Remote?
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: What is one advantage of remote work mentioned?
questions.explanation: Employees save commuting time.

questions.prompt: What solution does the writer suggest?
questions.explanation: The writer proposes a hybrid approach.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_b: Although meetings are useful, they differ.
questions.option_c: Therefore, a mixed system may work.
questions.option_d: Although remote work is useful, but offices matter.
questions.explanation: Do not pair although with but.

passages.content_text: Some employees prefer working from home because they save commuting time and can organize their day more independently. In my opinion, remote work can be very effective for tasks that require concentration. However, offices still have advantages. For example, new employees may learn faster when they can ask colleagues questions in person. Although online meetings are useful, they do not always create the same sense of connection. Therefore, a mixed system may be a practical solution for many companies. Employees could work from home on some days and meet in the office when collaboration is important.

topics.title: Narrating Events and Everyday Communication
topics.objective: Tell clear stories about past events using sequencing, appropriate tense choices, and practical communication.
topics.theory: A clear narrative often combines past simple, past continuous, sequencing expressions, and descriptive details. Useful sequencing words include first, then, while, suddenly, after that, eventually, and finally.
examples: First, we checked the map.
While we were walking, it started to rain.
Suddenly, the lights went out.
Eventually, we found the hotel.

common_mistakes.wrong: Suddenly, we were found the station.
common_mistakes.correct: Suddenly, we found the station.

common_mistakes.wrong: While we walked for hours, the phone rang once.
common_mistakes.correct: While we were walking, the phone rang.

questions.prompt: Which word often introduces an unexpected event?
questions.explanation: Suddenly introduces an abrupt event.

questions.prompt: Which word can introduce the last step?
questions.explanation: Finally commonly marks the last event.

questions.prompt: Complete: While we ___ for the hotel, it started to rain.
questions.explanation: The search was in progress.

questions.prompt: Choose the best sequence.
questions.explanation: These words organize a narrative.

questions.prompt: Complete: Suddenly, the bus ___ and everyone got off.
questions.explanation: The sudden completed event uses past simple.

questions.prompt: Read: 'While we were waiting, a taxi finally arrived.' Which event was in progress?
questions.explanation: Waiting was ongoing.

questions.option_d: Finally, we were found the hotel.
questions.explanation: Use 'we found the hotel'.

questions.prompt: Which word means 'after some time or difficulty'?
questions.explanation: Eventually often signals the final result after delay or difficulty.

questions.explanation: The train stopped unexpectedly.

questions.prompt: How did the story end?

passages.title: A Difficult Journey
passages.instructions: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: Why did they stop at the service station?
questions.option_b: Heavy snow made the road difficult to see
questions.explanation: Snow reduced visibility.

questions.prompt: Who showed them another route?
questions.explanation: A local driver helped them.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is incorrect?
questions.option_c: They were waiting at a service station.
questions.option_d: They eventually were reached the village.
questions.explanation: Use 'They eventually reached the village.'

passages.content_text: Last winter, three friends decided to spend a weekend in a mountain village. They left the city early on Saturday morning. At first, the journey went smoothly, but while they were driving through the hills, heavy snow began to fall. The road became difficult to see, so they stopped at a small service station. While they were waiting there, a local driver explained that the main road had been closed. He showed them another route on a map. After that, they drove more slowly and carefully. Eventually, they reached the village two hours later than planned. Although the journey had been stressful, they were relieved to arrive safely and enjoyed the rest of the weekend.

passages.title: A Lost Wallet
passages.instructions: Listen carefully and answer the questions.

questions.prompt: When did the speaker notice the wallet was missing?
questions.explanation: The speaker noticed while getting off.

questions.prompt: Who had found the wallet?
questions.explanation: A passenger found it and gave it to the driver.

passages.audio_text: I was getting off the bus when I realized my wallet wasn't in my pocket. First, I checked my bag. Then I called the bus company. Luckily, a passenger had found it and given it to the driver. I picked it up later that afternoon.
